       1             SENATOR MARCELLINO:  Good morning.

       2             My name is Senator Carl Marcellino, and I

       3      represent the 5th Senate District on Long Island,

       4      and I am the Chairman of the Senate Committee on

       5      Investigations and Government Operations.

       6             And, I thank you for coming.

       7             The purpose today is to examine the issue of

       8      the use of, or alleged use of, automated sales

       9      suppression devices to evade New York State sales

      10      tax.

      11             The hearing will investigate the use of the

      12      so-called "tax-zapper" software that let's

      13      businesses, especially that those that deal mostly

      14      in cash, to underreport taxable sales and pocket

      15      money that should be given to state and local

      16      governments.

      17             These crimes, if occurring, hit our residents

      18      twice:  First, when they properly pay their sales

      19      tax and it's kept by the merchant; and, second, when

      20      the state and municipalities are short revenue, and

      21      have to cut services or personnel -- and/or

      22      personnel.

      23             So, some of my colleagues will be a little

      24      late.  The weather, and the conditions, getting up

      25      from the Island and New York City are slow, so we're





 

                                                                   4
       1      going to proceed ahead.

       2             The first speaker will be Nonie Manion, who's

       3      the director of the audit division for the New York

       4      State Department of Taxation and Finance.

       5             Welcome to you, and thank you for coming.

       6             NONI MANION:  Good morning.

       7             SENATOR MARCELLINO:  Good morning.

       8             NONI MANION:  My name is Nonie Manion.  I'm

       9      the director of the audit division.

      10             And on behalf of Commissioner Mattox, I want

      11      to thank the Chairman and members of the Committee

      12      for inviting the Tax Department to submit testimony

      13      on the issue of sales tax evasion conducted by the

      14      use of automated sales suppression devices.

      15             About $25 billion in state and local sales

      16      tax revenue was collected last year.  Most of this

      17      revenue, about 96 percent, is from vendors

      18      voluntarily complying with their obligations to

      19      collect and remit the revenue to the State.

      20             Recognizing that most vendors want to comply

      21      with their state tax obligations, the Department has

      22      recently begun an initiative to improve our guidance

      23      and communication with businesses.

      24             For example:  We offer best-practices

      25      guidance to help businesses understand the





 

                                                                   5
       1      recordkeeping obligations, and those things they

       2      need to know when starting or expanding a business

       3      in New York.

       4             Nevertheless, the Department conducts about

       5      35,000 sales tax audits annually, and issues over a

       6      billion dollars in assessments of sales and local

       7      sales tax -- of state and local sales tax.

       8             The Department of Taxation and Finance

       9      devotes a significant amount of audit and compliance

      10      resources to identify sales tax underreporting.

      11             One method of underreporting can be

      12      facilitated by software that may reside in a

      13      point-of-sales system, which is often referred to as

      14      "phantom-ware," or, be run from removable media,

      15      such as a CD or flash drive; i.e., a "zapper."

      16             Through our audits, we have discovered that

      17      functionality and a point-of-sale system that exists

      18      for legitimate purposes can be used by unscrupulous

      19      businesses intent on skimming sales tax collections.

      20             A cash register system may have the

      21      capability to void certain sales at the end of the

      22      day to account for, example, returned merchandises.

      23             Businesses that use this capability to,

      24      instead, pocket the cash received from the customer

      25      and eliminate any direct evidence by deleting the





 

                                                                   6
       1      sale, are misapplying the programming inherent in

       2      point-of-sale devices.

       3             The problem is compounded by suggestions from

       4      point-of-sale salespersons that functionality exists

       5      in their equipment in an attempt to close the sale

       6      to a potential customer.

       7             While the underreporting of sales tax may be

       8      occurring through the use of these sophisticated

       9      technologies, it should be noted that evasion may

      10      also be committed by less-sophisticated methods that

      11      result in not recording the cash sales.

      12             Through our joint efforts with the

      13      Legislature, the Department has been granted some

      14      important tools to identify all types of sales tax

      15      underreporting.

      16             The 2009-10 State budget enacted requirements

      17      that certain third parties file annual information

      18      returns with the Tax Department.

      19             Under this law, franchisers must report

      20      yearly sales by their franchisees in the state, and

      21      alcoholic-beverage wholesalers must report the

      22      amount of sales made to bars, restaurants, food

      23      stores, liquor stores, et cetera, and insurers of

      24      motor vehicles are mandated to disclose payments on

      25      behalf of their insured to motor-vehicle repair





 

                                                                   7
       1      shops.

       2             This legislation is already providing

       3      results.  More than 500 vendors have been selected

       4      for audit using the third-party reports, and these

       5      audits have generated an additional $11 million in

       6      state and local sales tax.

       7             In addition, the 2009-10 budget required

       8      financial institutions to annually report, by

       9      New York State payee, their gross amount of settled

      10      payment card and third-party network transactions.

      11             The first report of this information was

      12      received by the Department earlier this year.  By

      13      comparing the third-party information to reported

      14      sales, the Department has an important tool to

      15      detect underreporting by cash-based businesses.

      16             Auditors routinely use this third-party

      17      information to validate whether the information

      18      captured by vendor's point-of-sale system or cash

      19      register is complete.

      20             To assist us in uncovering sales tax

      21      underreporting, the Tax Department staff have read

      22      the available literature on sales suppression

      23      devices, and studied the sales-recording module, or,

      24      "black box," approach taken by the Province of

      25      Quebec as a measure to thwart the zapper use in the





 

                                                                   8
       1      restaurant industry.

       2             This approach required the purchase of the

       3      sales-recording modules by each business, the cost

       4      of which was reimbursed by the provincial

       5      government.

       6             Each module costs about $800, plus

       7      installation fees.

       8             A number of states are looking to legislative

       9      options to address zappers.

      10             The Department is reviewing each of these

      11      approaches for their cost to implement, and their

      12      impact on the businesses that are regulated.

      13             Any enforcement approach must be carefully

      14      balanced in a manner that both maximizes voluntary

      15      compliance and minimizes the cost of doing business

      16      in New York.

      17             An unavoidable reality of tax administration

      18      is that some bad actors are determined to commit

      19      fraudulent acts and retain tax revenue.

      20             Use of automated sales suppression devices

      21      and software is an especially sophisticated way to

      22      commit this fraud, but constitutes one in a large

      23      number of tactics.

      24             We believe that the third-party

      25      information-reporting laws mentioned above provide a





 

                                                                   9
       1      powerful mechanism for the Tax Department to

       2      identify vendors that underreport sales, including

       3      those that may use the sales suppression software.

       4             We look forward to working in partnership

       5      with you on the matter, and thank you for the

       6      opportunity to appear before you today.
